title: Setting up on double-pointed needles
subtitle: Distributing stitches across four or five needles for small circumferences.
excerpt: Double-pointed needles (DPNs) allow knitting in the round on small circumferences such as socks, gloves, and hat crowns. This tutorial covers distributing the cast-on, joining without twisting, and working the first round.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter (1886), stocking-knitting series. Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), circular knitting chapter.

glossaryTerms.definition: Short knitting needles with a point at each end, sold in sets of four or five. Used to knit small circumferences in the round by distributing stitches across three or four needles and using the fifth as the working needle.

content.text: ) are the traditional tool for knitting small circumferences in the round. A set of four or five needles carries the cast-on stitches on three or four needles while the fifth is free to knit with. Socks, gloves, hat crowns, i-cord, and wrist warmers have all been knitted on DPNs since at least the eighteenth century. The setup looks precarious; the fabric locks the arrangement together within a few rounds. Difficulty: intermediate.
A set of 4 or 5 DPNs in the correct mm size
Cast all stitches onto one DPN using your preferred cast-on.

Slide the stitches along to distribute roughly equally across three DPNs (for a 4-needle set) or four DPNs (for a 5-needle set). The total stitch count guides the split: 48 stitches on 3 needles = 16 per needle.
Arrange the needles into a triangle (3-needle set) or square (4-needle set) with the cast-on edge sitting at the bottom of each needle.
Check that all stitches face the same direction and none are twisted around any needle. This is the join-without-twisting check.
Place a stitch marker at the beginning of the round if your pattern requires one.
Pick up the free DPN and knit across the first needle. When the first needle is empty, use it as the new working needle to knit across the second needle. Continue around.

DPNs appear in sock patterns, glove and mitten patterns, and hat patterns that work the crown separately before joining to the brim. Weldon's Practical Knitter prescribes four needles for all stocking work. Magic loop and two-circular methods have largely replaced DPNs in modern patterns, but many knitters prefer the shorter needles for hat crowns where magic loop becomes unwieldy.

items.symptom: Ladder of loose stitches at needle junctions
items.cause: Tension loosening where the working yarn transfers from one DPN to the next
items.fix: At the start of each needle, work the first two stitches slightly more tightly than usual and tug the yarn firmly before settling into the normal tension.

items.symptom: The work twists on the first round
items.cause: Stitches were twisted around one needle during setup
items.fix: Unravel back to the cast-on and re-distribute. Once even one round is worked, the twist is locked in and cannot be fixed without frogging.
